Fair challenge. Checking the source myself:
The local checkout is **142 commits behind `origin/master`**. The helper read that stale working tree, which uses LLVM `profraw` coverage. Checking current `origin/master`:

You're right, and the mistake was in what the helper read. Your local Quicksilver checkout is **142 commits behind `origin/master`**, and the helper read that old working tree, which still used LLVM `profraw` coverage. Current Quicksilver (`efe4b09`) works as you describe:
- It puts a small runtime switch at the start of every function and compiles the workspace once.
- The same switch records which tests enter which functions, giving a function-level map (`src/sitemap.rs`).
- Mapping is much cheaper: the README reports 1 h 5 min for Bifrost's C#/PHP/Ruby/Go analyzer scope on a 64-vCPU host, and 21 min for mbx.

**What that changes about the answer:** a function-level "entered" map supports a fairly clean rule. Rerun test Y when the diff edits the body or signature of any function Y entered. That rule has one useful property: adding a new function only matters if some existing caller is edited to call it, and that caller is in the map. The cases the switch can't see still need a conservative fallback:
- **Edits outside an instrumented function body.** Types, `const`/`static` items, trait impls (an added impl can change dispatch without a caller edit), `const fn`s and skip-attributed functions, which get no switch, and code generated by `macro_rules!`. These need crate-level reruns.
- **Runtime file reads.** Fixtures and goldens need separate per-test input tracking. That matters a lot for Bifrost, where master changes `tests/fixtures/` almost every hour.
- **Build and manifest changes** force a full rerun.

So the payoff depends on how often a master diff is "function bodies only" versus structural. Root suites link nearly every crate, so any structural edit in a shared crate like `bifrost-store` would trigger the crate-level fallback and rerun the root suites.

**Revised recommendation:** start with a cheap measurement that needs no builds. For the last few dozen promotions, classify each master diff into function-body-only edits, structural edits by crate, and fixture changes. Then compute what the rule would have rerun. If most promotions come out narrow, the next step is one real map on a batch candidate, replayed against `known_failures` to check that nothing would have been missed. Then a shadow mode in Attest.

Shall I run the diff-classification pass? It's pure Git analysis, delegated to a helper on the current `origin/master` sources this time.

**Result: a function-level map would almost never narrow promotion reruns for Bifrost.** The helper classified all 349 promotions merged Oct 22 – Nov 1:

| Category | Promotions | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Narrow (function bodies, fixtures and docs only) | 15 | 4.3% |
| Narrow if test-code edits are allowed too | 31 | 8.9% |
| Structural edit in a crate the root package links | 305 | 87.4% |
| Build or manifest change (full rerun) | 48 | 13.8% |
| Root-suite fallback either way | 307 | 88% |

- **The narrow promotions contain no production code.** All 15 were docs, fixture-only or empty diffs. Allowing test-code edits, only 3 promotions touch a single production function.
- **Structural edits pile up across master changes.** A promotion merges hours of master changes, so it nearly always contains several kinds at once:

  | Structural edit kind | Promotions containing it |
  |---|---|
  | Added or removed functions | 279 |
  | Impl changes | 240 |
  | Signature or attribute changes | 240 |
  | Struct changes | 203 |
  | `const` changes | 190 |

  Only 2 promotions fell back solely because of trivial top-level changes. So a smarter structural rule wouldn't rescue many: even if added functions were treated as harmless, struct, impl and `const` changes still force the crate-level fallback.

The broad conclusion is high confidence. The exact fractions are medium: the classifier is conservative where a change crosses function boundaries and can't see inside macro expansions. All changed Rust files parsed. The table is at `/tmp/qs-diff/promotions.csv`.

**My take:** Quicksilver's map is a good fit for mutation testing, but not for skipping post-promotion reruns here. For that, the real choice is policy, not tooling. After promotion, the agent could rebuild and rerun only previously failing checks and the plan's `rerun` entries outside the root suites. Interaction failures with master would then be left to master CI after landing, which async mode already relies on for slips. That would remove most of the second pass, roughly half of batch test time in the recent samples. The cost is more red master runs for triage and the fixer to clean up. I'd only do it if you're comfortable with that trade. Otherwise, the rerun plan deployed today is about as narrow as Cargo-level information allows.

> struct, impl and const changes still force the crate-level fallback

is there a way to fix this?

Yes, in principle. Add a static layer that says what each function's body *depends on*, next to Quicksilver's dynamic layer that says which functions each test *entered*.

**The rule:** test Y is affected by a change to item I when Y entered some function F whose body depends on I. "Depends on" covers:
- types it uses, including inferred ones;
- `const`s and `static`s it reads;
- trait impls its calls resolve to.

The dynamic map already captures everything reached transitively at run time, so the static layer only has to be precise one level deep, per function body.

**How that handles each edit kind:**
- **Struct or enum changes**, including `#[derive]` and field edits, affect functions that construct, match, access or serialize the type. Inferred types matter: `serde_json::to_string(&x)` depends on `x`'s struct even though the struct is never named.
- **`const` and `static` changes** affect functions that read them.
- **Impl changes:** methods already have switches. Adding an impl matters only where code selects it by type or trait, which the static layer resolves. Removing one breaks compilation unless nothing used it.
- **Signature changes and new functions** force caller edits, which the map already covers.

**Where the static layer could come from:**
1. **rust-analyzer as a library** (`ra_ap_*` crates). It works on stable Rust, does full type inference per function body, and is computed once per tree.
2. **Bifrost's own Rust analysis.** That's dogfooding, and its answers flag incompleteness explicitly, so an `Incomplete` answer can fall back to a crate-level rerun for just that item.
3. **rustc's incremental dependency graph.** It's exact but needs nightly.

Proc macros, build scripts, manifest changes and fixture reads still need their own fallbacks or input tracking.

**The real risk is the shape of the dynamic map, not precision.** Bifrost's golden suites run the whole analysis pipeline, and master keeps editing core types in `bifrost-store`, `bifrost-core` and `bifrost-semantic`. If most golden tests enter the functions that depend on those types, the selection stays broad even with a perfect static layer. It would narrow well only for language-specific changes, such as a promotion that touches only the C# analyzer.

**The cheap, decisive test is to compute a lower bound before building any static layer:**
1. Build one Quicksilver map of the root suites on a recent batch candidate. The README's Bifrost scope took about an hour on 64 vCPUs; this host has 32.
2. For the 349 promotions, count the tests that entered any function whose *body* changed, ignoring structural edits entirely.
3. If that lower bound already selects most tests, no structural rule can help, and we stop. If it's small, building the dependency layer is worth it.

Investigating: pulling the recent triage announcements and the jobs behind them from the CI database.

**They aren't new problems. Triage re-reviews the same open performance tickets every morning, and the Slack message presents them as if they were new.** I checked the database and GitHub:

- **What happened today:** the daily Benchmark run (02:08 UTC, engine `bd0d8ba7`) reported 25 cases still running slower than their baseline. Triage split them into two investigations (13 and 12 cases), plus a third that hasn't posted yet. Each matched its cases to existing open `performance-regression` tickets.
- **What it did to the tickets:** it only commented. It created and reopened nothing. All 11 tickets are open: #3737 dates from Sep 29, #6397–#6399 from Oct 22, and the rest from Oct 28 – Nov 1.
- **Why the message looks like news:** the announcement ("triage: N product issues") lists updated tickets in the same way as new ones.
- **It has happened every morning since at least Oct 25.** There were 22 benchmark investigations in 8 days, two to four each morning. #6397 has been commented on 24 times, #3737 22 times, and several others 5–6 times.

**Why:** benchmark intake treats a still-regressing case on a new engine head as needing fresh review. That was deliberate, so a changed engine gets re-checked. But master moves every night, so every case that's still slow gets re-investigated, mapped to the same open ticket, commented on and announced again. The two or three investigations each morning also overlap on the same tickets.

**What I'd change (your call):**
1. **Don't re-review a regression that an open ticket already tracks.** Treat "still slow on a new head" as the same episode. Review again only if:
   - the measurement got materially worse;
   - the ticket was closed;
   - the case recovered and then regressed again.
2. **Announce only new or reopened tickets.** Updates to existing tickets would go in the thread at most, or nowhere.
3. **Merge each morning's benchmark observations into one investigation.** That ends the overlap across two or three jobs.
